These increased tax rates were initially passed by voters in 2012 during a budget deficit, and were extended by voters in 2016.
Each year, the high-income tax rates bring in between $5 billion and $15 billion for the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). The revenue has ranged year to year depending on earnings from the stock market and other outside factors. For those who earn over $1 million, that tax has been on top of another existing 1% tax that goes toward mental health services.
Former LAUSD Superintendent Austin Beutner, who founded Vision To Learn 12 years ago, is flanked by Sherlett Hendy Newbill, LAUSD School Board member, and David Goldberg, president of California Teachers Association, as Vision To Learn gives out its 300,000th pair of glasses in California at 24th Street Elementary School in Los Angeles on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026.
MediaNews Group/Getty Images David Goldberg, the president of the California Teachers Association, which supports the proposition, told CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) that if the measure doesn’t pass, about 50,000 teachers could be laid off.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The ballot measure also has support from the National Education Association and the California School Employees Association. The opposition includes the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
While Prop. 3 appears to be gliding toward a win, polls are showing that Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire tax, is on track for failure. That measure would impose a new, one-time 5% tax on the financial assets of anyone who is worth $1 billion or more. If passed, 90% of the money would go toward funding healthcare to make up for an estimated $30 billion California (https://www.chcf.org/blog/2025/10/03/how-massive-federal-cuts-will-create-unprecedented-challenges-medi-cal-patients-providers/) will lose every year for Medicaid after Congress cut funding. Another 10 % would go to public education, food assistance and administration of the tax.
Prop. 40 has seen support drop in recent weeks (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/polling-proposition-40-22496894.php) as billionaire-funded opposition efforts ramped up. The Public Policy Institute of California released a poll Tuesday that found the measure only has 46% of voters in favor of the billionaire tax. Another poll from SurveyUSA also found that only 44% of voters are in support.
A hand holds a political mailer about California Proposition 40, a November 2026 ballot measure proposing a one-time tax on billionaires, in Reliez Valley, California, Oct. 23, 2026.
Gado/Getty Images The No on Prop. 40 campaign has been primarily bankrolled by a political action committee called Building a Better California that was formed this year, largely focused on blocking the measure, according (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767) to state finance disclosures. With contributors like Google co-founder Sergey Brin, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison and billionaire investor John Doerr, the group has raised over $333 million, mostly going toward opposing Prop. 40 and supporting propositions 41 and 42, which would nullify Prop. 40 (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/prop40-billionaire-tax-poison-pill-22468923.php), making it one of the highest-funded ballot initiative efforts (https://news.ballotpedia.org/2026/10/26/with-798-9-million-in-contributions-and-counting-2026-is-the-most-expensive-ballot-measure-election-cycle-in-california/) in California history.

Proposition 41 would require audits of special statewide taxes and prohibit certain types of new taxes, and Proposition 42, which is endorsed by Gov. Gavin Newsom and other Democrats, would block new taxes on the ownership of most financial assets, and would block new state taxes that apply retroactively to taxpayer conduct.
The Institute of Governmental Studies poll released Thursday surveyed 2,787 registered voters, of which 1,477 had either already voted in the midterm election or were considered likely to vote. It was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 19 through Oct. 25, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

5 tax measures are on the California ballot. Here’s how to make sense of them all
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)
October 5, 2026 October 4, 2026
Republish
Share this:
Share on X (Opens in new window)
X (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/tax-propositions-ballot-measures/)
Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)
Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/tax-propositions-ballot-measures/)
Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window)
WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/tax-propositions-ballot-measures/)
Mayra Joseph, a teacher at Sylvia Mendez Elementary School in Berkeley, joined members of the California Teachers Association and supporters of public education in a march to the Capitol as part of RedForEd Day of Action in Sacramento on May 22, 2019. Photo by Rich Pedroncelli, AP Photo
In summary
California voters haven’t had to make so many decisions about tax policy at the ballot since 1990. Our analysis shows voters tend to reject new taxes.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
California voters will soon be asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And they’ll be asked whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They’ll also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.
Just the right amount of news
Just the right amount of news
Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed.
Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed.
Email address
By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/).
Sign up for free
Δ
Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

arguments.query: Prop 3 passes California voters make high-earner income tax permanent

content.text:
1. What to know about California's other tax-the-rich measure
https://www.almanacnews.com/calmatters/2026/10/21/what-to-know-about-californias-other-tax-the-rich-measure-prop-3/
Prop.
3 would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services.
It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016.
Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031.
...
Prop.
3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually.
It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners.
Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes.
Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3%, the highest in the nation.
The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges.
If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund.
...
3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
...
If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Gold

2. Your last-minute guide to Proposition 3, the other tax-the-rich measure
https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-30/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-last-minute-voter-guide
# Your last-minute guide to Proposition 3, the other tax-the-rich measure
## The basics
Proposition 3 would make an expiring state income tax on high earners permanent.
## The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are.
Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers.
Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
...
### Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
...
## Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners.
In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030.
Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved.
The state could expect to lose $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

3. Your last-minute guide to all California propositions
https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-31/la-me-all-california-propositions-last-minute-voter-guide
Voters will decide on proposals to tax billionaires, extend taxes on high earners, fund biomedical research and more on the November general election ballot.
...
## Proposition 3
...
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich.
But almost all of it centers around Proposition 40, the heavily contested billionaire tax, and two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
But Proposition 3 — getting far less attention — also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40.

What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3
by
CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)
October 21, 2026 5:00 am
Share on X (Opens in new window)
X (https://www.almanacnews.com/calmatters/2026/10/21/what-to-know-about-californias-other-tax-the-rich-measure-prop-3/)

Email (mailto:?subject=%5BShared%20Post%5D%20What%20to%20know%20about%20California%E2%80%99s%20other%20tax-the-rich%20measure%3A%20Prop.%203&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.almanacnews.com%2Fcalmatters%2F2026%2F10%2F21%2Fwhat-to-know-about-californias-other-tax-the-rich-measure-prop-3%2F&share=email)
This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last.
Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031.
“I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.”
Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners.
Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation.
The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund.
Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges.
In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said.
Union’s big push
The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.”
The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500.
The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did.
Prop. 3 is not the only tax-the-rich measure (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/tax-propositions-ballot-measures/) on the Nov. 3 ballot. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said.
“We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said.
The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said.
‘Not sustainable’
Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/05/california-schools-funding-increases/) and declining enrollment (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2024/11/school-closures/).
“We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.”
In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016), the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes.
California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living.
Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students (https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202223_summary_2.asp), according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11.
That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now.
“Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.”
He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding.
“No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said.

Teacher Emily Adams’ eighth-grade science class at Lawson Middle School in Cupertino on Aug. 26, 2025. Only two weeks into the school year, students are doing basic exercises to familiarize themselves with lab instruments, learn the value of accuracy, and practice working together to build a foundation for the rest of the year.
Voters first passed the tax in 2012, then renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031.
If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last.
Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031.
“I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.”
Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners.
Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation.
The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund.
Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges.
In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cut

Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

Educators Fear California’s Flood of Ballot Initiatives Could Sink School Funding Measure
Proposition 3 would extend a tax on the state’s highest earners, preserving a key source of revenue for school districts across California.
Evgeniy Shkolenko/Getty Images.
Published
on
October 8, 2026
By
Mark Kreidler (https://capitalandmain.com/author/mkreidler)
Share
California’s Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm) , an ongoing tax on top income earners to help fund the state’s massive public education system, faces virtually no organized opposition. A September survey found that it enjoyed 58% support (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) among likely voters. It doesn’t create a new levy, either; it simply takes a tax that has been on the books since 2012 and makes it permanent.
So why are the measure’s supporters so nervous?
For the answer, look no further than a sample ballot for California’s Nov. 3 election. It’s bulging with 14 statewide propositions (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures), five of them involving tax questions of some kind.
That list includes Prop. 40, the so-called Billionaire Tax (https://capitalandmain.com/billionaires-shouldnt-exist-why-california-unions-are-fighting-for-a-wealth-tax), by far the largest and most controversial of the lot, along with two propositions that are expressly written to derail Prop. 40 if it is approved. And all of those measures were leading in the September survey by the Public Policy Institute of California, even though two of them are diametrically opposed to the third.
That’s a pretty solid sign that voters are baffled by the array of choices facing them. And for the teachers’ unions who say Prop. 3’s tax money is essential to the state’s education funding and some of their own members’ jobs, that is a worrisome place to be.
“While there’s no actual campaign against Prop. 3, I think a lot of people are confusing the ads against Prop. 40 and carrying that over to Prop. 3,” said Jeff Freitas, president of the California Federation of Teachers, which represents 120,000 education workers in the state. Freitas added that the CFT’s own polling numbers have come in lower than the robust showing in the September survey.
For those and other reasons, the CFT and the 310,000 strong California Teachers Association are rallying their members and using their money to help get out the vote in favor of Prop 3. (Disclosure: Both unions are financial supporters of Capital & Main.)
Their concern is understandable. At stake is $10 billion or more (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/) in education funding and essential services each year, a significant chunk of the state’s annual allocation for public schools from pre-K through community college.
“It’s a priority situation that we’re dealing with,” Freitas said.
* * *
California voters first passed a tax on high earners to safeguard education funding in 2012, when the state was facing heavy revenue losses following the Great Recession. Four years later, voters chose to extend the tax through 2030. Prop. 3 would remove the expiration date altogether.
The tax itself is straightforward: a slightly higher rate on the state’s top 2% (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016) of earners. In fiscal year 2025, that meant it applied only to individuals earning more than about $371,000, or $743,000 for married couples filing jointly, according to research (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/) by the California Budget & Policy Center.
Prop. 3 is also a tax on income only, not overall wealth. That’s an important distinction from the proposed Billionaire Tax, whose aim is to generate $100 billion in revenue over five years (primarily for health care funding) by placing a 5% one-time levy on the total net worth of the state’s roughly 250 billionaires.
But while proponents of the Billionaire Tax are only estimating what the state might receive from that measure, those pushing Prop. 3 have a clear idea about what the education tax revenues are worth. While the amount collected will vary, Freitas said the tax has been reliably worth $8 billion to $12 billion in annual public education funding in recent years.
That is upward of 10% of the state’s annual education budget. It has been a major boost. But that’s also what makes the prospect of Prop. 3 failing so concerning to the unions who represent hundreds of thousands of school teachers and support staff — and it’s the reason they’re not willing to take any chances.
* * *
The California Teachers Association has spent more than $33 million (https://edsource.org/2026/wealth-tax-vs-income-tax/767043) to qualify Prop. 3 for the ballot and rally support for it, and the California Federation of Teachers has added nearly $2 million more. Both unions are mobilizing their members to walk precincts and work phone banks as the vote draws closer.
In September, the CTA organized more than 1,000 of its members up and down the state to canvass neighborhoods and knock on doors. The goal was not only to talk up Prop. 3’s benefits, but to help voters distinguish it from the other tax measures on the November ballot.
The CTA includes on its website a tool that estimates how much funding (https://www.cta.org/our-advocacy/school-funding/yeson3) would be lost in each of California’s school districts if the tax extension fails. (Los Angeles Unified School District alone would be in line for a hit of more than $838 million per year.) The CTA estimates that one in six educators’ jobs would be at risk if the funding goes away.
There’s no ad campaign opposing Prop. 3. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which believes in strictly limiting government taxation, has weighed in against it (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/proposition-3-is-a-warning-against-proposition-40/), arguing that the education tax was created as a temporary measure in 2012 and touted again as temporary when it was renewed in 2016.
“The real lesson here is that whatever is represented to voters about a ballot measure seeking new programs or higher taxes should not be taken at face value,” Jon Coupal, president of the Jarvis association, wrote in a column (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/proposition-3-is-a-warning-against-proposition-40/) published on the organization’s website. Prop. 40, Coupal argued, should be viewed warily partly because of Prop. 3’s history.
It’s that conflation of tax measures — arguing against Prop. 40 and Prop. 3 at the same time, for example — that most concerns union leaders about the education tax’s chances of passage. And as the voters’ muddled response to the Public Policy Institute of California’s September survey demonstrated, there already appears to be plenty of mixed messaging out there.
“We’re getting school boards to pass resolutions [of support] for Prop. 3, we’re providing materials to our members, and we are definitely getting out there,” said CFT’s Freitas. It may take all that and more to ensure that the education tax doesn’t get lost in the shuffle come November.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The well-funded campaign for Proposition 3 describes it as a direly needed tool for funding public schools.
“Prop. 3 maintains critical funding for local schools, preventing larger class sizes and teacher layoffs,” says a video ad on YouTube. “Every dollar goes to local schools, not politicians in Sacramento.”
In reality, the ballot initiative is another tax measure on high-income Californians, this one helping to pay for all state services supported by general fund dollars, including healthcare, courts and schools. In other words, schools are the sales pitch to voters for a tax measure that affects considerably more than schools.
Advertisement
The measure has huge support from California’s largest teachers union, and it is separate from Proposition 40, the billionaire tax measure. No one is staunchly fighting Proposition 3 — including the group of billionaires who would rather see it pass than 40.
Proposition 3 would make permanent higher tax rates on about the highest-earning 2% of the state’s tax filers, rates that would otherwise expire at the end of 2030. If these tax rates were allowed to expire, the state’s general fund would absorb a massive annual hit of an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in today’s dollars.
Of the money raised by this tax, about 40% goes to funds that pay for transitional kindergarten through community college. About 60% goes to other areas — healthcare, in-home supportive services, higher education, the prison system, the court system and more. That explains why a broad coalition of unions supports the Yes on Proposition 3 campaign, even if the overriding pitch is about schools.
Advertisement
The biggest spender in support of Proposition 3 is the California Teachers Assn. — which poured about $60 million into promoting it through Monday and has harnessed its vast membership for on-the-ground canvassing. The teachers union has embraced Proposition 3 as a more strategic alternative to Proposition 40, which a mid-September poll (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-25/la-me-berkeley-poll-september-propositions-billionaires-wealth-tax)found has divided likely voters.
Support has been strong for Proposition 3, although public polling also has been more limited.
Propositions 40 and 3 each would benefit schools. But the teachers union is uncomfortable with how Proposition 40 is structured. Union leaders also worry that two tax-the-rich measures could confuse voters and turn them against both — especially given the massive campaign billionaires are waging against Proposition 40.
“When you have hundreds of millions of dollars being spent against the idea of raising revenue, I think that does impact the general voter zeitgeist,” said CTA President David Goldberg. “There’s always a fear that voters can get overwhelmed and confused, and voters can just say, ‘I’ve had enough,’ and just vote against everything.”
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on many assets of California billionaires who lived in the state as of Jan. 1. It is projected to raise tens of billions of dollars — mostly for healthcare. Prop. 40, in some respects, is a direct, albeit temporary, response (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/more-than-351-million-spent-on-wealth-tax-on-november-ballot) to phased-in health- and social-service cuts in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed in July 2025.
For educators, said Goldberg, Proposition 3 is the better bet than Proposition 40 because a greater percentage of 3 goes to education and its benefit would be ongoing.
Advertisement
“The funding for Prop. 3 has become a huge and an essential part of our education funding in California,” Goldberg said. “Making it permanent is vitally important. We are a labor-intensive kind of work, so potentially up to one in six educators could be looking at layoff notices at the end of this decade. And the impact would be felt even earlier as districts would start to prepare and hold back reserves.”
Other donors of $1 million or more (https://project-voter-guide-2026.interactives.calmatters.org/general/en/campaign-finance/prop/3) to Yes on 3 include, as compiled by a CalMatters database: National Education Assn.; California School Employees Assn.; CFT — a separate California teachers union; and the California arm of the Service Employees International Union as well as SEIU Local 2015, which represents in-home care providers and nursing home staff.
It adds up to more than $81 million for and about $5,500 against.
Odd bedfellows
In a case of odd bedfellows, Building a Better California, the billionaire-funded group bankrolling the fight against the billionaire tax, has endorsed Proposition 3.
Proposition 3 keeps rates billionaires already pay on income — and appears likely to pass — while Proposition 40 would, in total, subtract billions from their net worth. Their explanation (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/faq) is that “we believe in strong, accountable investments that will strengthen our state, protect our schools, address the housing crisis, and improve other essential public services.”
CTA is far from alone in choosing Yes on 3 (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQu1D6GLGe_Yqu1kHb_AGUtbd&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhHMTHFZTUZlUHflSSg6z_2CXI42u6UpgvyIXvgUGaQdt3raGu_PPbhoCid0QAvD_BwE) and No on 40 (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVZHnSZ3kD_EdGrqvCLqPITgu&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhN0sUpdT8Pt04p0vK6yHMXKobIYGrXAwVzXAt3Dm7_oGx_Ifu5UY8BoCZ7QQAvD_BwE). Others in that camp include California Medical Assn., California Professional Firefighters, United Domestic Workers, Gov. Gavin Newsom and gubernatorial front-runner Xavier Becerra.
The main No on 40 committee is fronted by doctors, teachers, firefighters and unions, but nearly 100% of its money has come from Building a Better California, the group overwhelmingly funded by tech billionaires.
Advertisement
Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone had given $102 million as of late October to stop the billionaire tax, per a data analysis by Capital & Main (https://capitalandmain.com/who-are-the-billionaires-behind-the-304-million-effort-to-defeat-californias-wealth-tax); CTA has given nothing, according to Goldberg.

“California’s schools, hospitals, and clinics need funding. Billionaires do not,” said Julie Van Winkle (https://yeson40.com/another-public-education-union-backs-prop-40-the-california-billionaire-tax/), a vice president of United Teachers Los Angeles.
A no position on both propositions was taken by the California Republican Party, Libertarian Party and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn.
Opponents of Proposition 3 point out that an original campaign pitch of the higher tax rates, back in 2012, was that they would last only through 2018 “to address a budget deficit,” according to the No on Prop. 3 website (https://votenoprop3.com/). “Those ‘temporary’ taxes were later extended, and now politicians want to make them permanent. California voters deserve real results, not broken promises.”
Advertisement
Richard Barrera, a liberal Democrat and school board member whom CTA is endorsing for the office of state superintendent of public instruction, supports both propositions. His opponent, conservative Republican Sonja Shaw, also a school board member, opposes both.
The Proposition 40 funding adds up to (https://project-voter-guide-2026.interactives.calmatters.org/general/en/campaign-finance/prop/40) $33.4 million for and $130 million against.
What does Proposition 3 do?
The higher rates were originally to last through 2018. An accompanying sales tax increase was in place for four years. A major selling point was that the higher tax rates were temporary.
The sales tax was allowed to sunset. But the higher tax rates were extended through 2030 by voters who approved Proposition 55 in November 2016.
In 2011, the state tax brackets topped out at 9.3%. Starting in 2012, the temporary tax created brackets of 10.3%, 11.3% and 12.3%. If Proposition 3 fails, the highest state tax rate in California would revert to 9.3% in 2031, although still on the books would be an unrelated additional 1% surcharge on taxable income over $1 million for mental health services.
Who falls into the higher brackets — in terms of income — has been adjusted upward over the years for inflation.
The 10.3% rate affects individual filers with taxable income from $371,479 to $445,771. That bracket for married couples filing jointly is $742,958 to $891,542.
Advertisement
The top 12.3% rate applies to single filers with taxable income above $742,953 and joint filers above $1,485,906.

California's proposed billionaire tax has commanded most of this election's attention, but a less-talked-about tax measure appears to be one of the few statewide tax propositions that is likely to succeed.

## Proposition 3
Proposition 3 would make a state income tax on high earners permanent.
If passed, tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are.
Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers.
Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners.
In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030.
Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there will be grave problems if the measure is not approved.

But this time might be the last.

It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016.

Blog Post · November 2, 2026
Five Fast Takes on California’s Midterm Mood
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Stephanie Barton , (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Across the country and in California, Election Day is nearly upon us. More than 23.2 million Californians have registered to vote—in past election years, over 80% said they planned to vote (https://www.ppic.org/blog/who-are-californias-infrequent-voters-and-when-do-they-vote/). Californians entered the midterm in a dark mood, but has their gloom convinced them to cast their ballots? We look at the voter numbers and what issues set the mood during this election cycle.
1. The voters you might expect to vote early, did vote early. By the end of October, over 5 million registered voters (https://politicaldata.com/early-vote-counts?districtId=9999&districtName=California%20Statewide) had returned a ballot, a higher number than in the days leading up to the June primary. But ballots have arrived at a pace to be expected for a midterm. While other states across the country may have seen a surge in early voting, that bump may be due to voters who would typically vote on Election Day (https://www.npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6012308/midterm-elections-early-voting-data).
Democratic voters have led the charge of returning ballots early, sending over 2.5 million. Republicans have returned nearly 1.5 million, and independents have sent in more than 1 million ballots. In familiar fashion, older voters and white voters have made a very strong showing—these voters constitute the bulk of early returns.
2. Young and old are eying the same gubernatorial candidate. Democrat Xavier Becerra has led in the polls since earning one of the top two spots in the governor’s race with Republican Steve Hilton. Today, Becerra claims 61% support from likely voters to Hilton’s 37% support. Over seven in ten young likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/priorities-for-californias-young-voters/) indicate they would vote for Becerra, as do well over half of voters over 50 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf). Hilton remains very popular with Republican voters, underscoring the notion that most Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) consider their candidates acceptable options.
3. The tax on billionaires has lost its appeal though the permanent tax on high earners has not. Today 46% of likely voters support Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time tax on Californians with assets over $1 billion, with fewer Democrats (64%) than a month ago (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (72%) now saying they would vote yes. Meanwhile a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would extend a marginal income tax on Californians earning over $371,000. Back in September, people had grumbled about the excessive ballot measures (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/); this October, many (88%) praised the voter information guide from the Secretary of State as useful in deciding how to vote on the many initiatives.
4. Some Californians see voting as a light in the dark mood. Eighty-two percent of California adults nurse a dim view of the direction of the US, and 77% are pessimistic about California’s economic outlook. Views that housing costs are a big problem (64%), incomes are not keeping up with inflation (76%), and disapproval of US military action in Iran (75%) have further hardened attitudes.
Yet as seven in ten likely voters question the state of democracy in the US, Democratic likely voters (71%) are more enthusiastic than usual about voting for Congress, compared to 46% of Republicans. This enthusiasm comes amid new congressional districts created through redistricting that favor Democrats, where few competitive races (https://www.ppic.org/blog/the-mix-of-political-views-in-californias-new-congressional-districts/) remain among the 52 House seats up for grabs. Amid heavy disapproval of Congress (82%) and of President Trump (78%), it is no shock that 63% of likely voters intend to vote for the Democrat in their district.
5. Voters do not extend much grace to the political parties themselves, but they trust the system. In September, only 41% of likely voters felt the Democratic Party had at least some good ideas (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-0926.pdf); fewer (27%) granted the benefit of the doubt to the Republican Party. Despite this lack of faith in parties, the people still believe in the process that defines democracy: six in ten likely voters have a good deal of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections.
Although midterms have been known for their lackluster turnout, the issues and candidates this year have managed to capture the state’s attention. Voter enthusiasm and voter confidence during the 2026 election cycle may well boost the numbers at the polls.

### Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering.
874,641 valid signatures were required.
The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents.
These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 through 2030.
Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent.
Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets.
The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.

Ballots arriving in peninsula mailboxes this week carry an open governor’s race, 14 statewide propositions — among them a one-time 5% tax on billionaires and two competing measures that would cancel it — and an Assembly seat that two Democrats are vying to fill.
...
This roundup covers the state and federal contests: the offices first, then the propositions.
Each of the 14 propositions needs a simple majority to pass.

## Governor: Becerra vs. Hilton
*State official, all voters*
Gov.
Gavin Newsom is termed out, and the race to succeed him pits Democrat Xavier Becerra, a former U.S. Health and Human Services secretary, California attorney general and longtime Los Angeles-area congressman, against Republican Steve Hilton of Atherton, a former Fox News host and onetime senior adviser to British Prime Minister David Cameron.
Becerra led the June 2 primary statewide with 28%, ahead of Hilton’s 24.6%.
In Marin, Becerra ran second to Democrat Tom Steyer, who did not advance, while Hilton drew 14.2%.
A Republican hasn’t won the governor’s office since 2006.

content.thinking:
No results are in yet, so this is being asked before the vote. I'm weighing base rates: California tax measures have mostly failed since 2000, though extensions of existing taxes, like Prop 55, have done better. I also note that support for propositions usually slips as Election Day nears.

I'm checking the polling against the counterarguments: Prop 3 held near 58% in PPIC and 54% in IGS through late October, and even the anti-Prop 40 group endorsed it. CFT's internal numbers came in lower, but still likely above 50%. The electorate also leans Democratic with a strong enthusiasm edge, so the majority support looks solid.

I'm settling on the Yes side as the more likely winner, but I want to recheck the Berkeley IGS subsample of people who've already voted, and see whether SurveyUSA has any Prop 3 numbers.

**yes**

The election is November 3, 2026, and I couldn't find any results yet. Every signal I found before the vote points to Prop 3 passing:

- **Polls:** Every poll had Yes above 50%, and support held steady into late October. PPIC had it at 58–40 in September and 58–41 in mid-October. Berkeley IGS had it at 54–37 in late October, the only one of seven measures it tested with majority support. A third poll, by AIMSA, had 56% Yes.
- **Money:** The Yes side raised about $81 million, mostly from the California Teachers Association. The only committee opposing it reported $5,500, and there was no ad campaign against it.
- **Endorsements:** Supporters include Gov. Newsom, Xavier Becerra (the leading candidate for governor), the state Democratic Party and major unions. Even the billionaire-funded group fighting the separate billionaire tax (Prop 40) endorsed Prop 3. Opponents include the Republican Party, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and CalTax.
- **History:** Voters approved the same tax in 2012 with 55.4% and extended it in 2016 with 63.3%. Renewing an existing tax tends to do better than proposing a new one.
- **Political mood:** Democrats were more enthusiastic about voting this year, and about 80% of them supported Prop 3.
- **Betting markets:** On October 29, Kalshi gave it a 95% chance of passing and Polymarket 94%.

**Risks:** California tax measures often fail, and support for propositions tends to slip near Election Day. There were five tax measures on this ballot, so voters may have been tired of them or confused with Prop 40. A rival teachers union said its own polling showed lower support than PPIC's. None of these looked big enough to erase Prop 3's lead.
